name: The two women before Solomon
charge: Two harlots, one living child, and a claim that only a sword could sort out
summary: Two harlots who lived in one house each bore a son three days apart; one woman’s child died in the night because she lay on it, and she exchanged it for the living child while the other slept (1 Kings 3:16-22). There was no witness, and before the king each claimed the living child. Solomon called for a sword and ordered the child divided; the true mother gave up her claim to save the child’s life, the other would have it cut in two, and the king gave the child to its mother, so that all Israel saw the wisdom of God in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:23-28).
offenseFull: The case came before the throne soon after Gibeon, when Solomon had asked for an understanding heart to judge the people and to discern between good and bad (1 Kings 3:9). Two women who were harlots stood before the king. The first said that she and the other woman lived in one house, that she gave birth there, and that three days later the other woman gave birth as well, with no one else in the house but the two of them. The other woman’s child died in the night because she lay on it. She rose at midnight, took the living son from beside the first woman while she slept, laid him in her own bosom, and laid her dead child in the first woman’s bosom. In the morning the first woman rose to nurse her child and found him dead, but when she looked closely in the light she knew it was not the son she had borne (1 Kings 3:16-21). The teaching notes that a child dying under its sleeping mother is something that happens, and it hurts the mothers greatly; and that to an untrained eye one small baby can look like another, but a mother knows her own.

The other woman answered that the living child was hers and the dead one belonged to the first, and the first said the opposite, and so they argued before the king (1 Kings 3:22). How was Solomon to know who was lying and who was telling the truth? He was king over all Israel and did not know these women. There was no stranger in the house to bear witness, both women claimed the same right, and both laid the dead child on the other. The classes add that during the time of Solomon, the Kingdom of Heaven on earth, there were still harlots, and they came to the king in a pair: all flesh keeps company with its own kind.
judgmentFull: The king repeated both claims back to them, called for a sword, and when it was brought he ordered the living child divided in two and half given to each (1 Kings 3:23-25). Then the woman whose child it was spoke, because her heart yearned over her son. She begged the king to give the other woman the living child and by no means kill it. The other said to let it be neither hers nor her rival’s, but divided (1 Kings 3:26). The teaching reads the second woman plainly: she did not care whether the baby was put to death, because she had already lost her own; she wanted company in her misery. It compares her spirit to that of women today who have abortion after abortion and have no love for the child. The king answered that the living child was to be given to the first woman and by no means killed, for she was its mother (1 Kings 3:27).

The Jurisprudence class asks what law Solomon had to go on, since no statute covers one woman taking another’s baby, and answers that he went on the strength of common sense. From the moment he called for the sword he knew the real mother would react in a way the false one would not; he judged by what he had seen of a mother’s love for her child. Wisdom knows things of old and can conjecture aright what is to come; she knows the subtleties of speeches (Wisdom of Solomon 8:8). Conjecture is a conclusion formed on incomplete information, and Solomon had only each woman’s version of the story; by wisdom, experience and the law he reached a right conclusion and recognised the subtlety in the false woman’s speech. Most in the congregation will never be judges, the class says, but they still have to understand judgment, and study is how that wisdom is gained.

All Israel heard of the judgment the king had judged, and they feared the king, for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him to do judgment (1 Kings 3:28). This was the answer to what he had asked at Gibeon, made visible to the whole nation through a household dispute between two women. The Lesser and the Greater class then turns to Christ, the greater Solomon, who did not need anyone to testify of man, for he knew what was in man (John 2:24-25). Solomon had to hear the women out and watch their countenance; Christ perceives the thoughts of men before they speak (Luke 5:22). The record gives no separate punishment for the false claimant. It ends with the living child given to his mother.

text.text: Then came there two women, that were harlots, unto the king, and stood before him.
And the one woman said, O my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house; and I was delivered of a child with her in the house.
And it came to pass the third day after that I was delivered, that this woman was delivered also: and we were together; there was no stranger with us in the house, save we two in the house.
And this woman’s child died in the night; because she overlaid it.
And she arose at midnight, and took my son from beside me, while thine handmaid slept, and laid it in her bosom, and laid her dead child in my bosom.
And when I rose in the morning to give my child suck, behold, it was dead: but when I had considered it in the morning, behold, it was not my son, which I did bear.
And the other woman said, Nay; but the living is my son, and the dead is thy son. And this said, No; but the dead is thy son, and the living is my son. Thus they spake before the king.
Then said the king, The one saith, This is my son that liveth, and thy son is the dead: and the other saith, Nay; but thy son is the dead, and my son is the living.
And the king said, Bring me a sword. And they brought a sword before the king.
And the king said, Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other.

Then spake the woman whose the living child was unto the king, for her bowels yearned upon her son, and she said, O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it. But the other said, Let it be neither mine nor thine, but divide it.
Then the king answered and said, Give her the living child, and in no wise slay it: she is the mother thereof.
And all Israel heard of the judgment which the king had judged; and they feared the king: for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him, to do judgment.

And God said unto him, Because thou hast asked this thing, and hast not asked for thyself long life; neither hast asked riches for thyself, nor hast asked the life of thine enemies; but hast asked for thyself understanding to discern judgment;
Behold, I have done according to thy words: lo, I have given thee a wise and an understanding heart; so that there was none like thee before thee, neither after thee shall any arise like unto thee.
